title: The Witch Who Judged Sunshine
markdown:
Witch Juniper’s cottage smelled of dried lavender and chamomile that had been taken seriously. Green hills rolled up as if they liked the sky. She kept days tidy: sun, pollen apron, herb beds, smudged spellbooks, a wave to a passing cloud sprite. Excitement was a twisty root or extra-fluffy cheese scones. She liked the steady version of living.

A puffing messenger brought a scroll in a floppy ribbon that had already given up being smart. Judge, annual Sunpetal Festival. Woven sunlight. Singing flowers. An old secret rule nobody remembered, which was the sort of rule that liked to arrive late and look important. Moths of unease in her stomach, the kind that do not ask. She set a scone down unfinished. She was good at moonpetal temperature, at knowing when chamomile had steeped long enough to forgive you, not at being esteemed, not at noise, not at standing where a thousand eyes expected a verdict that sounded like a law.

Before a polite refusal could dress itself, a second messenger, wobbly sun-seal: if the judge failed to appear, first cancellation in memory, a ten-year shadow on the mountain country, sunpetals drooping, singers silenced. Steam-sigh. Shadowed silence was worse than jitters. She packed the rocky-path boots and a basket of calming teas. Cricket the goblin trotted, knobbly knees, eyes for shine. “Festivals are shiny and loud, aren’t they?”

The path to Oakhaven was rock and thin air and Cricket naming every gleam as if gleam were a census. Juniper drank tea from a lid and did not hurry, which was her only rebellion. The town clung to the mountainside like goats with opinions. Market: banners arguing with wind, baskets, herbs that tickled, a thousand conversations stacked like plates, distant flower-bells practising for the real thing. A child offered her a petal and ran. Not cottage quiet. Her apron, in the square, felt like a costume.

Day one of judging was a fog in official clothing. Elder Meadowbrook’s beard had its own agenda. He muttered about the sacred flicker.

“What is that?”

“The flicker. Essential.” He stopped, as if the word had done the work.

Cricket collected stream pebbles that winked. “Maybe a sparkly stone. It flickers.”

Villagers brought sunlight-woven baskets that glowed as if they had swallowed afternoon, tiny warm suns on stands, choruses of flowers that kept trying to outdo the next stall and then laughing when they failed. Juniper tasted a crumb of festival cake she had not meant to accept. She felt the old pull home, boots ready to reverse, the cottage a neat answer to a messy question. Frozen almost, spectacles sliding, Elder’s flicker still unexplained. Then the thought of silent beds, a square without song, ten grey years because she had liked her own kettle too much. She looked properly: shimmer on petals, honest laughter, a grandmother teaching a boy how to twist a stem so it held. Not a forgotten clause. A togetherness with leaves. Cricket’s pebbles clicked in the pouch like a second, smaller jury.

Last day, wind in her apron, Cricket proud of his geology, the Elder creased with importance. “Not the most perfect weave or the loudest song,” Juniper said, hands a little honest. “Elara. A sun-warmed daisy chain. Biggest smiles. Warmest hugs.”

Surprise, then a buzz. A daisy chain.

Meadowbrook sputtered. “The sacred flicker is a sunbeam in a dewdrop through a unicorn’s eyelash.” Dusty parchment, autumn-brittle. “See.”

The writing was spider-faint: moonlight, badger fur, a grumpy toad. Not Oakhaven’s memory. A rule so hidden it had never lived here. The quiet after was heavy. She could perform the silly rite and please the beard. Cricket’s pouch weighed comfort. Elara beamed in a knot of proud people.

Stomach twist, the old moths again, a sour taste of wanting to please a beard and a seal. Then she looked at Elara, at Cricket’s lighter future, at the cake crumb still on her own thumb. “History,” Juniper said, gentle and not moving. “The festival I saw is joy today. Perhaps the flicker was the light in her face.” Rough paper under the fingertip, fibres whispering, old-ink smell like a cupboard that had been closed on purpose. She could have tried moonlight and toad. She tucked the parchment beside the teas instead. “A piece of the past. Not the heart.” Meadowbrook’s beard settled, slowly, as if it too had been outvoted. Someone clapped. Then more. The daisy chain, in the late sun, did a perfectly ordinary shine.

They walked home under orange-pink-purple peaks that did not require a judge. Cricket’s pouch was lighter; children of Oakhaven now flickered in their own right, pockets clicking. He hummed a tune that had not applied for a licence. Behind them the square kept being happy without a unicorn’s eyelash. Juniper’s basket held teas, seeds she had bought without needing, and a parchment that would live in a drawer marked History, Not Homework.

Days later, seeds, ink fingers. A golden blur at the window: a young sunsprite, lost, a captured beam with opinions. She opened the casement, herb air going out. “Lost?” A crystal-chime sound. It landed on her finger, warm trust, no parchment required. She did not name it magic. She showed it the path the hills already knew.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
